name: Osteotomy for lengthening

lead: An osteotomy for lengthening is the surgical cut that begins a limb-lengthening procedure. The surgeon divides the bone, either completely (an osteotomy) or only through its hard outer shell (a corticotomy), and fixes a device to the bone on either side of the cut. For appearance, this is the first stage of cosmetic stature lengthening, in which the femur or tibia is extended to make a person taller or to change leg-to-torso proportions.

After the cut, the bone ends are held still for about a week and then slowly pulled apart, roughly a millimetre a day, while new bone forms in the gap. This principle is called distraction osteogenesis and was developed clinically by Gavriil Ilizarov. A systematic literature shows meaningful gains in height with good reported satisfaction, but also real complication rates.

paras: In general terms the sequence has four phases: the bone cut and device fitting under anaesthesia; a latency period of about a week when the device is inactive; a distraction phase in which the device lengthens the bone gradually; and a consolidation phase while the new bone hardens, followed by device removal in some systems. Devices include external fixators and internal lengthening nails, sometimes combined with plates. Surgery is done by specialist limb-reconstruction teams, and physiotherapy runs throughout.

Reported complications include pin-site or deep infection, bone that heals poorly or not at all (nonunion), bone healing at the wrong angle, hardware failure, nerve injury, muscle and joint contractures, and knee or ankle stiffness. Recovery takes many months. Regulators in some countries have restricted cosmetic use; China's health ministry banned the procedure in 2006 after serious adverse outcomes were reported. Anyone considering it would discuss risks with an orthopaedic surgeon experienced in limb reconstruction.

angle.text: The cut allows the bone to be lengthened in a controlled way, which adds permanent height to the leg segment treated. People use it as the surgical starting point of cosmetic stature lengthening, often to gain several centimetres.

lead: An osteotomy for lengthening is the surgical division of a bone that begins limb lengthening. The bone is cut either completely or only through its hard exterior (a corticotomy), and a lengthening device is attached to each side of the cut so the pieces can later be separated gradually while new bone fills the gap [1][2].

In looksmaxxing, the term most often refers to the first stage of cosmetic stature lengthening, where the femur (thigh bone) or tibia (shin bone) is cut and extended to add height, and to related procedures such as clavicle lengthening that change body proportions. Members of forums such as T Nation have discussed clavicle lengthening and the published case series on it [3].

The same cut-and-distract principle is used in medicine to correct short or deformed limbs, jaw hypoplasia and bone defects. Published studies in this area are mostly case series and retrospective reviews of medical lengthening, which orthopaedic teams have described as having both advantages and disputed details such as the osteotomy level, lengthening rate and complications [4][5][6].
infobox: About 1 mm per day after a latency of about 7 days [1]

paras: In limb lengthening the osteotomy is the first phase. The surgeon cuts the bone completely or only through the cortex, and fixes a device on either side of the cut [2]. A latency phase of about a week then follows with the device inactive, allowing early healing, before distraction begins [2].

Distraction is usually about 1 mm a day, divided into two steps. Descriptions of the technique note that too rapid separation can lead to nonunion, where unstable fibrous tissue forms instead of bone, while too slow a rate can allow the bone to fuse prematurely [2]. A consolidation phase follows, during which the device keeps the bone stable while it heals; some systems then require a second operation to remove the device [2].

Lengthening has been done with external fixators, with fully implantable motorised nails, and with combinations of nails and plates. Descriptions of manual external devices mention a rod turned to separate the bone, while implantable motorised nails are credited with less scarring and lower infection risk [1]. A Malaysian series on submuscular plates after femoral lengthening reported that the plate shortened the period in an external fixator, with mean lengthening of 5 cm in eight cases [7].

Other bones can be treated with the same principle: reviews have covered lengthening of metacarpals and phalanges with closed osteotomy, callus lengthening and modified Ilizarov methods [4], and a review of short-bone lengthening has examined results and complications [6].

Bernhard von Langenbeck first proposed the idea in 1869, and Alessandro Codivilla published the first clinical attempts in 1905, treating 26 people with malformed legs; complication rates were high and his methods were not adopted [1][2]. Beginning in the 1950s Gavriil Ilizarov studied the technique extensively, developed external fixators and defined the separation rates that made it widely usable [1][2].

Use in the jaw was pioneered by Wolfgang Rosenthal in 1930 but was not explored further until the 1980s, and a first modern-era paper on clinical jaw use appeared in 1992 [1]. Cosmetic stature lengthening for people of normal stature developed later and, according to published descriptions, has had high demand in India, where the industry is unregulated, while China's Ministry of Health banned limb lengthening in 2006 after serious side effects [1].

Most published work concerns medical rather than purely cosmetic indications. A single-surgeon series of congenital short femur lengthening used the Ilizarov technique and reported outcomes and complications [8]. A review of short-bone lengthening by distraction osteogenesis likewise reported results and complications [6]. In the eight-case femoral series using submuscular plating, lengthening averaged 5 cm (range 3 to 9 cm); one patient needed quadricepsplasty for restricted knee flexion and three had transient knee stiffness that resolved with physiotherapy [7].

Reported complication rates in distraction osteogenesis literature include infection of about 5 percent, bone growing in an undesired direction in 7 to 9 percent, and hardware failure in 3 to 4.5 percent, with nerve injury and nonunion also described [2]. Authors reviewing the field have noted that the osteotomy site, the length and speed of lengthening and postoperative complications remain disputed, and that long-term results of different methods need more study [4].

Documented problems include infection, malunion and nonunion, hardware failure, nerve injury, tooth-bud and facial-nerve injury in jaw procedures, and joint contracture [1][2][7]. Reports from India describe some patients who needed further surgery to walk again and others who gained less height than expected [1]. Recovery involves months of reduced mobility and physiotherapy.

Within height-focused communities, the osteotomy is discussed as the defining step of limb lengthening, the one surgical route that permanently adds height. Forum members also discuss related cuts in other bones, such as clavicle lengthening for shoulder width, and compare published case series [3].

timeline.event: Bernhard von Langenbeck proposes surgical bone lengthening [1].
Alessandro Codivilla publishes the first clinical attempts, in 26 people with malformed legs [1][2].
Wolfgang Rosenthal pioneers use of the technique in the jaw [1].
Gavriil Ilizarov begins the work that standardises distraction rates and external fixation [1][2].
First modern-era paper on clinical jaw distraction is published [1].
China's Ministry of Health bans limb lengthening after serious side effects [1].
